activities.name: cbBondSort

config.prompt: File each description under the bond type that behaves that way:

items.label: electrons transferred outright; rigid crystals of charged ions
a shared pair counts toward both outer shells
outer electrons pooled into a common sea
conducts only when molten or dissolved
conducts as a solid by drifting electrons
small discrete molecules or vast networks
cleaves when one layer slides a position

config.why: Transfer, share, pool — each route to the full-shell target builds a material with its own personality.

activities.anchor: never to use hairdryers in the bath
activities.caption: run the conduction test yourself — what does each result mean?
activities.name: cbCircuitBranch

config.root: You are handed a white crystalline solid with a high melting point. Run the tests and read the verdict.

start.text: The unknown solid sits on the bench. Where do you start?

choices.label: Clip it into a circuit as-is
choices.feedback: The lamp stays dark — nothing is carrying charge in this state.

choices.label: Skim the melting-point data first
choices.feedback: It melts above 1,000 °C — overcoming the attractions between billions of oppositely charged ions is expensive.

meltingData.text: Melting point: well over 1,000 °C. A hint about strong electrostatic attraction — but not yet a verdict.

choices.label: Now clip it into a circuit as-is
choices.feedback: The lamp stays dark — strong attractions alone do not move charge.

solidResult.text: No current through the solid. What next?

choices.label: Melt it and test the melt
choices.feedback: The lamp lights — mobile carriers appear at high temperature.

choices.label: Dissolve it in water and test the solution
choices.feedback: Conducts well — which is the household warning about electricity and the tub.

meltResult.text: Solid: dark. Molten: light. Melting point above 1,000 °C. Verdict: an ionic compound — conduction needs mobile charge carriers, and only melting frees the ions to move.

solutionResult.text: Dissolved: conducts. Solid: does not. Verdict: ionic — water pries the ions off the crystal and cages them, freeing the carriers.

config.why: Conduction needs mobile charged particles; ionic solids lock theirs in place, and only melting or dissolving frees them.

activities.caption: call the count inside one visible grain
activities.name: cbGrainEst

config.prompt: A single visible grain of table salt — roughly how many NaCl building blocks does it contain?
config.why: About 10¹⁸ of them — and that repeating cubic array is what a grain's little-cube habit shows through.
config.context: NaCl is a ratio, not a molecule: the smallest whole-number recipe for the whole crystal.

activities.anchor: its poles pry ions off the lattice and cage them
activities.caption: fill the blanks — placing a bond on the line
activities.name: cbPolarCloze

config.text: An electronegativity difference over about %%0%% means effectively ionic; between roughly 0.4 and 1.7 the bond is covalent but %%1%%; under about 0.4 it is essentially pure covalent. And the molecule's %%2%% shape keeps the two ends from cancelling — hence overall dipoles.
config.hint: O–H differences are 1.24 — squarely in the middle band; the shape is what stops water's poles cancelling.

activities.caption: pair each network with what its architecture buys
activities.name: cbNetworkMatch

config.prompt: Pair each structure with the properties its architecture gives:

pairs.right: four-bonded tetrahedral network — the hardest natural material, an insulator, a superb heat conductor
flat honeycomb sheets that slide — conducts along its layers; electrodes and motor brushes
every silicon bridged to four oxygens — the backbone of glass and rock, melting near 1,710 °C
same atoms, different bonding, wildly different properties

config.why: Diamond versus graphite is the showcase: composition identical, properties opposite — architecture, not ingredients, decides.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the alloying story
activities.name: cbAlloySpot

config.prompt: A student summarises the electron-sea model and alloying. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: Metals conduct because outer electrons drift through the piece when a voltage is applied.
The same mobile electrons carry kinetic energy, which is why metal feels cold to the hand.
Layers of ions slide past each other without breaking the bonding — metals bend instead of shattering.
Alloying adds same-sized atoms that make the lattice even more slippery, so steel is softer than pure iron.
Free electrons responding to light's electric field give metals their mirror finish.
config.correction: Alloying adds differently sized atoms — carbon into iron, copper into gold — that JAM layer-sliding: alloys are harder than pure metals, usually less conductive and less malleable.
config.why: Uniform lattices slide; irregular ones jam. Pure 24-carat gold is soft precisely because its lattice is perfectly uniform.

activities.anchor: Resist the temptation to sort bonds into three boxes
activities.caption: true or false — the continuum view
activities.name: cbSpectrumJudge

statements.s: An F–F bond shares its electrons perfectly evenly.
statements.why: Identical pullers — the neutral reference point at one end of the sharing continuum.

statements.s: A Na–Cl bond is best described as two atoms sharing electrons very unevenly.
statements.why: Sharing is abandoned altogether there — we talk about ions, Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

statements.s: A difference over about 1.7 means the bond is effectively ionic.
statements.why: Between roughly 0.4 and 1.7 it is covalent but polar; under about 0.4, essentially pure covalent.

statements.s: Even 'ionic' compounds are purely ionic: lithium iodide dissolves only in water, as a pure ionic model predicts.
statements.why: Lithium iodide dissolves in organic solvents — even ionic compounds carry partial covalent character.

activities.anchor: A quick decision procedure for the exam and the lab
activities.caption: put the bond-type recipe in working order
activities.name: cbDecisionOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the recipe from ingredients to verdict, in order:
items: Look at the ingredients: metal + non-metal, two non-metals, or metal + metal
Two non-metals → think covalent (molecular, unless it is diamond/graphite/quartz-type)
Metal + metal → think metallic, or an alloy
Predict properties from the model, then check: high melting and conducts when molten → ionic; low melting, no conduction → molecular covalent; bends, conducts as a solid → metallic
config.why: Ingredients first, model second, property check last — the same loop chemists run on every unknown.
